'''John R. Myhill Sr.''' (11 August 1923 – 15 February 1987)<ref>''Revue philosophique de Louvain'', Volume 85, 1987, p. 603.</ref> was a British [[mathematician]].

==Education==
Myhill received his Ph.D. from [[Harvard University]] under the supervision of [[Willard Van Orman Quine]] in 1949.<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=13713}}.</ref>  He was a professor at [[State University of New York|SUNY Buffalo]] from 1966 until his death in 1987.  He also taught at several other universities during his career.

His son, also called John Myhill, is a professor of linguistics in the English department of the [[University of Haifa]] in Israel.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://english.haifa.ac.il/index.php/en/component/contact/contact/37-faculty-staff-reception-hours/27-senior-academic-staf/82-jm?Itemid=424|title=Prof. John Myhill|website=english.haifa.ac.il|language=en-GB|access-date=2021-04-05}}</ref>

==Contributions<!--'Russell–Myhill paradox' and 'Russell–Myhill antinomy' redirect here-->==
In the theory of [[formal language]]s, the [[Myhill–Nerode theorem]], proven by Myhill<ref>{{cite report | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QjZwISLU4rAC | author=John Myhill | title=Finite automata and representation of events | institution=Wright Air Development Center | type=WADC Report TR | number=57–624 | year=1957 }}</ref> and [[Anil Nerode]],<ref>{{cite journal | jstor=2033204 | doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-1958-0135681-9 | url= | author=Anil Nerode | title=Linear Automaton Transformations | journal=[[Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society]] | volume=9 | number=4 | pages=541&ndash;544 | year=1958 | doi-access=free }}</ref> characterizes the [[regular language]]s as the languages that have only finitely many inequivalent prefixes.

In [[computability theory]], the [[Rice–Myhill–Shapiro theorem]],<ref>{{cite book
 | last = Rosenberg | first = Arnold L.
 | contribution = 9.5 The Rice–Myhill–Shapiro Theorem
 | doi = 10.1007/978-0-387-09639-1_9
 | location = New York
 | pages = 165–169
 | publisher = Springer
 | title = The Pillars of Computation Theory
 | year = 2009}}</ref> more commonly known as Rice's theorem, states that, for any nontrivial property ''P'' of partial functions, it is [[Undecidable problem|undecidable]] whether a given Turing machine computes a function with property ''P''. The [[Myhill isomorphism theorem]] is a computability-theoretic analogue of the [[Cantor–Bernstein–Schroeder theorem]] that characterizes the recursive isomorphisms of pairs of sets.

In the theory of [[cellular automata]], Myhill is known for proving (along with [[Edward F. Moore|E. F. Moore]]) the [[Garden of Eden theorem]], which states that a cellular automaton has a configuration with no predecessor if and only if it has two different asymptotic configurations which evolve to the same configuration. He is also known for posing the [[firing squad synchronization problem]] of designing an automaton that, starting from a single non-quiescent cell, evolves to a configuration in which all cells reach the same non-quiescent state at the same time; this problem was again solved by Moore.

In [[constructive set theory]], Myhill proposed an axiom system that avoids the [[axiom of choice]] and the [[law of the excluded middle]], known as [[Constructive set theory#Intuitionistic Zermelo–Fraenkel|intuitionistic Zermelo–Fraenkel]]. He also developed a constructive set theory based on natural numbers, functions, and sets, rather than (as in many other foundational theories) basing it purely on sets.

The '''Russell–Myhill paradox'''<!--boldface per WP:R#PLA--> or '''Russell–Myhill antinomy'''<!--boldface per WP:R#PLA-->, discovered by [[Bertrand Russell]] in 1902 (and discussed in his ''[[The Principles of Mathematics]]'', 1903)<ref name= IEP>{{cite IEP |url-id=par-russ |title=Russell's Paradox}}</ref><ref>{{cite SEP |url-id=russell-paradox |title=Russell's Paradox |first=Andrew David |last=Irvine |date=2016}} "The reason is that in Appendix B Russell also presents another paradox which he thinks cannot be resolved by means of the simple theory of types."</ref> and rediscovered by Myhill in 1958,<ref>"Problems Arising in the Formalization of Intensional Logic." ''Logique et Analyse'' 1 (1958): 78–83</ref> concerns systems of logic in which logical propositions can be members of classes, and can also be about classes; for instance, a proposition ''P'' can "state the product" of a class ''C'', meaning that proposition ''P'' asserts that all propositions contained in class ''C'' are true. In such a system, the class of propositions that state the product of classes that do not include them is paradoxical. For, if proposition ''P'' states the product of this class, an inconsistency arises regardless of whether ''P'' does or does not belong to the class it describes.<ref name=IEP/>

In [[music theory]], [[Myhill's property]] is a mathematical property of [[musical scale]]s described by John Clough and Gerald Myerson and named by them after Myhill.
